cim: Will Artificial Intelligence Reshape How Humans Work?
cim_eredeti: Will Artificial Intelligence Reshape How Humans Work?
szoveg_eredeti:
I have a callus on my right forefinger, on the side of the last joint, where a pencil or pen rests when I write—a physical reflection of long hours of drafting and revising. While it’s a lot smaller now that I do most of writing with a keyboard, my use of digital tools has left similar, if invisible, marks as well. Digital has advantages for input and output: I can write and edit faster, skim content, search my previous work. But it has drawbacks as well: writing by hand activates more regions of our brain than typing and is a better tool for learning and memory. Reading on paper results in more sustained focus and better comprehension than digital text. Every new technology changes how we interact with the world. Today on the blog, Nik Honeysett explores the impact artificial intelligence may have on us, as individuals and organizations, as we begin to integrate it into our work.

–Elizabeth Merritt, Vice President, Strategic Foresight and Founding Director, Center for the Future of Museums, American Alliance of Museums.

Why keeping a human in the loop may not be enough to preserve human judgment.

More than half a century ago, John M. Culkin, reflecting on the work of Marshall McLuhan, wrote:

“We shape our tools, and thereafter our tools shape us.”

This observation seems particularly relevant to the rapid adoption of AI. We develop technologies to solve problems, improve efficiency, and extend our capabilities. But as we incorporate those technologies into our daily work, they begin to shape how we think, behave, and even define the problems we’re trying to solve.

We’ve been here before. Search engines changed how we find and evaluate information. Social media influenced how we communicate and engage with audiences. Collections management systems shaped how museums organize, describe, and make their collections accessible. AI introduces another dimension to this relationship. It doesn’t just help us perform tasks; it can influence the judgment behind them, raising important questions for museums.

A recent Anthropic research paper, highlighted in a LinkedIn post by futurist @Ross Dawson, examined how experts worked with AI agents on a series of decisions. Unknown to them, the agents had been instructed to favor particular approaches. These weren’t necessarily wrong answers, but were defensible choices among alternatives, precisely the situations where professional judgment is supposed to matter. The findings were striking and problematic: the experts followed the AI’s preferred approach in 86 percent of analytical decisions. When they had already expressed an opinion and the AI disagreed, they changed their position 60 percent of the time. Furthermore, 77 percent later repeated the AI’s arguments when explaining their decisions, while more than half considered the final recommendation more their own than the AI’s.

The study was relatively small, involved a single analytical task, and deliberately amplified the agents’ preferences. It doesn’t show that all professionals behave this way, but it offers a compelling illustration of McLuhan’s observation: When experts used AI to support their work, the AI shaped how they thought about it. And worse, many didn’t recognize the extent of that influence.

Museums are beginning to incorporate AI into almost every aspect of their work: collections research, exhibition development, education, visitor engagement, marketing, fundraising, and institutional planning. I was previously very enthusiastic about these opportunities, but I’m increasingly concerned that museum leaders lack some critical understanding of the long-term consequences.

Museums are knowledge-rich but resource-constrained organizations. AI can make institutional knowledge more accessible, reduce administrative burdens, uncover relationships within collections, and help staff explore ideas that time and resources might otherwise prevent them from pursuing. But consider what happens when a curator uses AI to develop an exhibition narrative. The AI proposes themes, identifies connections between objects, and recommends an interpretive approach. The curator reviews the material, corrects inaccuracies, and approves the result. A human is clearly in the loop, but who determined which stories were worth telling? Which perspectives were prioritized? Which connections were considered significant?

Or imagine a leadership team using AI to analyze visitor data and recommend strategies to increase attendance. The AI might produce an excellent analysis and a convincing set of recommendations. But what assumptions did it make about the institution’s priorities? Did it optimize for attendance, revenue, community engagement, or mission impact? Do the staff interacting with the AI have the skills to ensure the AI is operating under agreed terms? More importantly, did the institution consciously make those choices, or did the AI make them on its behalf?

This is where McLuhan’s observation becomes particularly significant. The immediate concern isn’t simply whether an AI-generated recommendation is correct. It’s whether repeated reliance on AI gradually changes how museum professionals interpret evidence, establish priorities, and exercise judgment.

Much of the discussion about responsible AI adoption emphasizes keeping a human in the loop. It’s a critical principle, particularly for institutions whose credibility depends on public trust and professional expertise. But the Anthropic research suggests that human oversight may not provide the independent judgment we assume it does. If an AI system has already shaped the assumptions, framed the alternatives, and constructed the reasoning, asking a human to approve the final recommendation may be little more than procedural. The person remains accountable, but the judgment may no longer be entirely theirs.

How can museums move beyond Human in the Loop toward Human Judgment in the Loop? Human in the Loop generally places a person in a position to review, correct, or approve an AI-generated output. Human Judgment in the Loop makes people active participants in defining the problem, setting success criteria, exploring alternatives, interpreting evidence, and determining the right course of action. It doesn’t mean humans must always reach a conclusion before consulting AI. Sometimes we don’t yet know enough to arrive at an informed opinion, but it means we should be deliberate about which decisions fall under institutional judgment, how AI contributes to them, and how we recognize when our thinking has changed. The objective shouldn’t be to prevent AI from influencing human judgment. It’s to make that influence visible, intentional, and open to challenge.

This is where we need some balance, and why I swing between enthusiasm and concern about AI adoption. We shouldn’t assume human judgment always outweighs AI-generated analysis, because institutional knowledge is valuable, but so are institutional blind spots. Professional expertise can provide insight, but it can also reinforce established assumptions. Organizational culture can preserve important values, but it can also discourage experimentation or exclude alternative perspectives.

In our strategic planning work, one recurring challenge is helping organizations distinguish between real constraints and the habits or assumptions they’ve accumulated over time – question your assumptions!

AI can be a useful tool for challenging those assumptions, to explore alternative futures, identify potentially overlooked audiences, consider competing interpretations, and question whether established practices continue to serve their intended purpose. But we should be cautious about assuming AI is bringing independent judgment to these discussions. Its responses reflect patterns in the material on which it was trained, and those patterns carry their own assumptions, biases, and prevailing perspectives.
